results.result: Transgenic mice expressing GCaMP6f specifically in exocrine acinar cells were successfully generated and validated, showing uniform expression in essentially all acinar cells with no expression in other cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C21 and C22 describe the generation and validation of the transgenic mouse model. The methodology is clearly described with appropriate citations (C21), and the specificity of expression is documented with imaging evidence (C22, Figure 1C). This provides a solid foundation for the in vivo imaging experiments.

results.result: Electrical nerve stimulation at 1-100 Hz induced frequency-dependent increases in intracellular Ca2+ in acinar cells, with minimal response at 1 Hz, progressive recruitment at 3-10 Hz, and specificity confirmed by lack of contralateral gland response.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 and C27 collectively demonstrate frequency-dependent Ca2+ responses with appropriate controls. The data show clear dose-response relationships (Figure 2A,B) and the contralateral control (C27) provides strong evidence for neural specificity rather than direct electrical stimulation of acinar cells. Sample sizes are stated (n=4 fields from 4 animals).

results.result: Saliva secretion was absent at 1-3 Hz stimulation, progressively increased at 5-10 Hz, and showed a strong linear correlation (r²=0.995) with peak Ca2+ increases at moderate stimulation intensities (0-10 Hz).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 establish a clear relationship between stimulation frequency, Ca2+ signals, and functional output (saliva secretion). Statistical significance is reported with appropriate tests, sample sizes are provided (n=4 animals), and the strong correlation (r²=0.995) between Ca2+ and secretion is well-documented (Figure 3). This is a key functional validation of the physiological relevance of the Ca2+ signals observed.

results.result: Sustained saliva secretion requires both Ca2+ release and Orai-dependent Ca2+ influx, as demonstrated by GSK7975A significantly attenuating the plateau phase but not the initial peak of the Ca2+ response during prolonged 10 Hz stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 demonstrate the requirement for store-operated Ca2+ entry. The pharmacological approach using GSK7975A is appropriate, with vehicle controls included. The selective effect on the plateau phase (C32) versus the initial peak (C33) is consistent with the proposed mechanism. Data are shown in Figure 4 with statistical analysis (paired t-test, p<0.05, n=3-5 animals).

results.result: Grid-based analysis revealed that at 1 Hz stimulation, only 34% of sub-regions responded with prolonged latency (6.72±0.79 s), while at 10 Hz virtually all regions (98.5%) responded with minimal latency (1.70±0.27 s) and increased amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 describe detailed spatial and temporal characteristics of Ca2+ responses using a systematic grid-based analysis. The methodology is clearly described (8x8 grids, 32x32 μm), validated in supplementary data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and shows progressive recruitment and amplitude increases with stimulation frequency. Sample sizes are adequate (n=19 fields from 8 animals) with appropriate statistics (ANOVA with Tukey test).

results.result: Regions that responded strongly at low stimulus intensity (1 Hz) also showed the largest responses at higher frequencies, with high-responding regions exhibiting linearly enhanced increases (R²=0.9197) as stimulation strength increased.
results.evaluation: Claims C38 and C39 demonstrate spatial heterogeneity in responsiveness across the tissue. The analysis showing that the same regions are most responsive across all frequencies (Figure 6D) and the linear relationship (R²=0.9197) are well-documented with appropriate sample sizes (n=4-5 fields from 4 animals). This reveals important spatial organization of the Ca2+ signaling system.

results.result: Physostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor, enhanced Ca2+ signal amplitude following nerve stimulation, with effects becoming statistically significant at 3 Hz and above, confirming acetylcholine as the primary mediator of the observed Ca2+ responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 provide pharmacological evidence for cholinergic mediation of the Ca2+ signals. The dose-response relationship and frequency-dependent effects are well-documented (Figure 7) with paired experimental design (n=5 fields from 4 animals) and appropriate statistics (paired t-test). This validates that the observed signals reflect physiological neurotransmitter release.

results.result: At physiological stimulus strengths (particularly 5 Hz), Ca2+ signals consisted of brief (<2 s), repetitive, highly localized increases confined to the apical portions of cells within a few micrometers of the apical plasma membrane, in marked contrast to in vitro observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C43 and C44 describe a key finding that distinguishes in vivo from in vitro Ca2+ signaling. The spatial localization is clearly demonstrated through standard deviation imaging and time-lapse analysis (Figure 8). This represents a major departure from the global Ca2+ waves typically observed in isolated cells and is central to the paper's main conclusions.

results.result: At 10 Hz stimulation, Ca2+ signals initiated in the extreme apical ER established a standing apical-basal gradient, with basal Ca2+ reaching only ~20-30% (or ~25% by line scan analysis) of apical levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C45 and C46 quantify the spatial Ca2+ gradient at optimal secretion frequency. Multiple analytical approaches (standard deviation imaging, manual ROI analysis, line scans) converge on consistent measurements of the gradient (Figures 9 and 10). The line scan data (n=11 from 3 animals) with statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) provide robust quantification of this key finding.

results.result: Ca2+ oscillation frequency in vivo (~1 Hz) was markedly faster than in isolated cells (~0.2 Hz), modestly increased between 3 and 5 Hz stimulation, but showed weaker correlation with secretion (R²=0.824) compared to Ca2+ amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 characterize the temporal dynamics of Ca2+ oscillations using automated peak detection algorithms. The comparison between in vivo and in vitro frequencies is well-documented (Figures 11 and 12), with adequate sample sizes (n=13 fields from 5 animals for in vivo). The weaker correlation with secretion compared to amplitude (R²=0.824 vs 0.995) is an important mechanistic insight.

results.result: In acutely isolated GCaMP6f-expressing acini at 37°C, carbachol evoked Ca2+ oscillations (~0.2 Hz) that invariably initiated apically and globalized, with spatiotemporal profiles strikingly similar to previous reports using chemical indicators, ruling out the genetically encoded indicator as the cause of in vivo/in vitro differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 provide critical control experiments demonstrating that GCaMP6f properties do not explain the in vivo/in vitro differences. The isolated cell experiments at 37°C (Figure 12) show global Ca2+ waves consistent with prior literature, directly addressing a potential confound. Sample sizes are adequate (n=14-32 cells from 3 animals) with appropriate statistics.

results.result: A new mathematical model incorporating apical KCa channels and localized Ca2+ signals was developed, showing that optimal fluid secretion occurs when apical and basal KCa densities are approximately equal, and that absence of both propagated Ca2+ waves and apical KCa significantly decreases secretion.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 describe the development and key predictions of a revised mathematical model. The model incorporates the experimental findings (apical localization of Ca2+, presence of apical KCa channels) and makes testable predictions. The simulations show qualitative agreement with experimental data (oscillation frequency, spatial gradients, secretion rates). However, the model's predictive power would benefit from more quantitative experimental validation of specific predictions.

results.result: Previous work by the authors demonstrated that KCa3.1 and KCa1.1 channels, along with Na/K ATPases, are present in the apical plasma membrane of salivary acinar cells, with functional evidence from localized Ca2+ uncaging experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 summarize prior published work by the authors that provides crucial context for the current model. These are appropriately cited claims (Almássy et al., 2018; Almassy et al., 2012) that establish the presence and function of apical KCa channels, which is essential for interpreting the current in vivo findings. The claims are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: The failure of Ca2+ signals to propagate and the establishment of standing Ca2+ gradients are presumably due to efficient Ca2+ clearance by SERCA, PMCA, and mitochondrial buffering, preventing substantial CICR through IP3R and RyR distant from the apical trigger zone.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 proposes a mechanistic explanation for the localized Ca2+ signals, but this is explicitly speculative ("presumably"). While the proposed mechanism is plausible and consistent with known Ca2+ handling mechanisms, no direct experimental evidence is provided in this study to test this hypothesis. Future experiments manipulating these Ca2+ clearance mechanisms would be needed to validate this explanation.

results.result: The complex architecture of the salivary gland lobule is maintained by junctional complexes and extracellular matrix interactions, and enzymatic digestion during cell isolation may disrupt cellular polarity, potentially explaining altered Ca2+ signaling characteristics in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C65 and C66 propose that enzymatic isolation disrupts cellular architecture and polarity, leading to altered Ca2+ signaling. While C65 is supported by citation (Baker, 2010), C66 is explicitly speculative. The hypothesis is reasonable but lacks direct experimental evidence. Testing this would require comparing Ca2+ signaling machinery localization in intact versus isolated tissue, or using alternative isolation methods that preserve architecture.

results.result: Background claims establishing the current understanding of salivary secretion mechanisms, including the role of Ca2+ signaling, ion transporters, neurotransmitter pathways, and prior in vitro observations of global Ca2+ waves.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1, C2, C6-C20) provide essential background and context from the literature. They are appropriately cited and accurately represent the current state of knowledge in the field. These establish the framework against which the novel in vivo findings are compared. The claims are well-supported by the cited literature and represent accepted knowledge in the field.

results.result: In vivo nerve stimulation in live mice revealed that Ca2+ signals initiate in the apical ER but, in marked contrast to in vitro data, consist of highly localized transients that fail to fully propagate, establishing large apical-basal gradients at optimal secretion stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 summarize the main findings of the study as stated in the abstract. These are well-supported by the detailed experimental data presented in the Results section (Figures 8-10) and represent the core novel contribution of the work. The contrast with in vitro observations is clearly demonstrated through direct comparison experiments (Figure 12).

results.result: Local, non-propagating Ca2+ signals have been observed in isolated pancreatic acinar cells in response to IP3, low concentrations of secretagogues, and physiological concentrations of cholecystokinin.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 cites prior work in pancreatic acinar cells showing localized Ca2+ signals. This is appropriately cited (Ashby et al., 2003; Thorn et al., 1993; Thorn et al., 1996; Thorn and Petersen, 1993) and provides important context that localized signals are not unprecedented in exocrine cells, though the authors note important caveats about those studies (patch-clamp conditions).
